722.title: Shibboleth (Judges 12:1–6)
722.hook: a word said differently becomes a death sentence
722.howItsDone: Jews read the shibboleth story in Judges 12 as part of the Former Prophets, often alongside Gideon's soft answer to the same tribe in Judges 8 as a study in how a quarrel between kin grows or cools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jephthah's vow, a promise made in haste and kept at a terrible cost. Your line was rash vows cost. Today, Jephthah again, and a single word at a river.

A ford on the Jordan, where the river runs shallow enough to wade. Men of Gilead are guarding it. A traveler comes down to the water and asks to cross. Are you an Ephraimite? He says no. So they ask him to say one word. "Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right." That's all it takes. One sound, a little off, and they seize him at the water's edge.
screen: `A GUARDED FORD.` → `ARE YOU AN EPHRAIMITE?` → `SAY SHIBBOLETH.`

segments.voice: It starts with hurt pride. The men of Ephraim cross over to Jephthah after his victory, furious. Why didn't you call us to fight with you? We'll burn your house down over you. Ephraim made almost the same complaint once before, to Gideon, a few chapters back. Gideon answered softly: what have I done, compared with you? And their anger cooled. Jephthah answers with his own grievance, and then with war. Insults fly. The Gileadites win, and seize the fords so the Ephraimites can't get home. And at the river, the test isn't what you believe, or what you've done. It's how your mouth makes one sound. The word itself is ordinary. Elsewhere in the Bible, shibboleth is an ear of grain, in Pharaoh's dream of full and thin ears, and in a psalm it's a flood of water rising. Nothing holy about it. Just a word with a sh at the front that some people said as s. And these aren't foreigners at the ford. Gilead and Ephraim are kin, tribes of one people, descended in the story from the same family. That's the grief of it: brothers divided by an accent, and a word for grain turned into a test of who's in and who's out.

723.title: Samson's mother (Judges 13)
723.hook: the angel comes first to a woman whose name we never learn
723.howItsDone: Jews read Judges 13 as the haftarah for the Torah portion Naso, which contains the laws of the Nazirite, and rabbinic tradition pays close attention to Manoah's wife and gives her a name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shibboleth, an ordinary word for grain turned into a test at the fords of the Jordan. Your line was one word divides. Today, a new story, and it starts with a woman.

An angel of the Lord appears to a woman with no name. In the text she's the woman, his wife, Manoah's wife. She has no children. And the angel comes not to her husband, but to her. You will conceive and bear a son, he says. Drink no wine, eat nothing unclean, and no razor shall touch his head, for the child will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin to save Israel from the Philistines. The hero of the next chapters is Samson. But his story begins with her.
screen: `A WOMAN WITH NO NAME.` → `THE ANGEL COMES TO HER.` → `NO RAZOR ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: She goes and tells her husband. Manoah prays: let the man of God come again, and teach us what to do. The prayer is answered, and the angel comes again, but again to her, sitting alone in the field. Manoah isn't there; she has to run and fetch him. When he asks for the rules for the child, the angel's answer mostly points back to her: of all that I said unto the woman, let her beware. Manoah offers a meal, then asks the angel's name. The angel won't give it: a name withheld, in a story about a woman whose name we never learn. Then Manoah lays an offering on a rock, the flame goes up toward heaven, and the angel goes up in the flame. Manoah panics: we shall surely die, because we have seen God. And she reasons it through. "If the LORD were pleased to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and a meat offering at our hands." Nor would he have shown us all this, she says, or told us these things. She's calm, and she's right. The text leaves her nameless; the Talmud gives her a name, Tzlelponit. Either way, the order of the story is plain. The angel came to her, twice. She heard it first, and she was the one who understood it.

724.title: Delilah (Judges 16:4–21)
724.hook: strength given away a secret at a time
724.howItsDone: Jews read the Samson and Delilah chapters as part of the Former Prophets, and rabbinic commentary links Samson's strength to his Nazirite vow and asks why he gave his secret away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson's mother, never named, visited by the angel twice. Your line was the angel came to her. Today, her son is grown, and he falls in love.

In the valley of Sorek lives a woman named Delilah, and the lords of the Philistines come to her with an offer. Find out where Samson's great strength lies, and each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver. The text says Samson loved her. It never says she loved him. And she doesn't hide what she's doing. She asks him straight out: tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and how you could be bound.
screen: `SILVER FROM THE PHILISTINE LORDS.` → `SAMSON LOVED HER.` → `TELL ME WHERE YOUR STRENGTH LIES.`

segments.voice: He lies. Bind me with fresh bowstrings, and I'll be weak. She does, with men lying in wait in the room, and cries: the Philistines are upon you, Samson. He snaps them like thread. Again: new ropes, never used. He snaps those too. The third time, listen. Weave the locks of my hair into the loom. Still a lie, but drifting toward the truth: now it's about his hair. Then she presses him: "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me?" She pressed him daily, the text says, until his soul was vexed unto death. And he tells her everything. No razor has come on my head; I've been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. Some readers hear the strength living not in the hair itself, but in the vow his mother was given, with the hair as its sign. She lulls him to sleep on her knees and calls a man to shave him. When she cries, the Philistines are upon you, he wakes and thinks, I'll go out as at other times and shake myself free. Then the line that hurts: he did not know that the Lord had departed from him. Nobody took his strength in one blow. He handed it over a little at a time, each lie a step closer to the truth.

725.title: Once more (Judges 16:28–30)
725.hook: blind and chained, Samson prays for strength one last time
725.howItsDone: Jews read Samson's death in Judges 16 as part of the Former Prophets, often with the Mishnah's comment that Samson 'went after his eyes' beside the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Delilah, who asked again and again until Samson told her his secret. Your line was guard your strength. Today, Samson with nothing left to guard.

A prison house in Gaza. The Philistines have put out Samson's eyes, bound him in bronze chains, and set him to grind. The man who once tore a young lion apart with his bare hands now grinds grain for the people who blinded him. Then, almost in passing, the text drops in one sentence: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven." Nobody in the prison notices. The reader does.
screen: `GAZA: BLIND, CHAINED, GRINDING.` → `THE HAIR BEGINS TO GROW.` → `NOBODY NOTICES.`

segments.voice: The lords of the Philistines gather for a great feast to their god Dagon, and send for Samson to entertain them. The house is packed; people crowd the roof to watch. A boy leads him in by the hand, and Samson asks him something small: let me feel the pillars the house stands on, so I can lean on them. Then he prays. "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God." It isn't the first time he has called on God; once, dying of thirst after a battle, he cried out and water came. But through all the lions and snapped ropes, the text never shows him asking for strength. Now, blind and weak, he does. Remember me. Only this once. The text doesn't clean up his prayer, either. He asks to be avenged for his two eyes. The rabbis noticed. The Mishnah says Samson went after his eyes, following what he saw and wanted, and so it was his eyes the Philistines took. The tradition keeps both truths: a man whose own choices brought him here, and a God who still hears him when he asks. He braces against the two middle pillars, and the house comes down, and he dies with them. He asked, and at the end, the strength came.

726.title: Right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25)
726.hook: the book ends: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes"
726.howItsDone: Jews read the closing verse of Judges as the hinge into the books of Samuel, and commentators differ on whether it calls for a human king or laments a people who no longer answered to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, once more: Samson at the pillars, asking for strength only this once. Your line was only this once. Today, the book of Judges closes.

Here is the last verse of the book of Judges: "In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes." No song, no victory, no wedding. The chapters before it are hard to read: a private shrine with a hired priest, a tribe that carries off that shrine's idols and its priest, a crime in a city at night, and a war between the tribes that nearly wipes one of them out. Then that sentence, like a door closing.
screen: `NO SONG, NO VICTORY.` → `HARD CHAPTERS.` → `A DOOR CLOSING.`

segments.voice: The line has been coming back in those last chapters like a refrain: in those days there was no king in Israel. And the full sentence, everyone doing what was right in his own eyes, stands at both ends of those chapters, as they open, and as the very last line. The phrase has a history. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people that in the land they will not do as they do now, every man whatever is right in his own eyes. Instead, the Torah says, do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord. Same words, other eyes. There's an echo inside Judges too. When Samson first wants a Philistine woman, he tells his father, get her for me, and in Hebrew what he says is: she is right in my eyes. The man who went after his eyes, in a book that ends with everyone doing what was right in their own. What does the closing line want? Readers differ. Some hear a call for a king, and the next book brings one. Others remember that Gideon refused a crown, saying the Lord shall rule over you, and hear the problem as people with no one to answer to but themselves. Either way, in its telling, a person's own eyes are real, and they matter, but they are not enough by themselves.
screen: `NO KING IN ISRAEL: A REFRAIN.` · `DEUTERONOMY: NOT IN YOUR OWN EYES.` · `SAMSON: SHE IS RIGHT IN MY EYES.` · `A KING, OR GOD AS KING?`

727.title: Hannah's silent prayer (1 Samuel 1)
727.hook: a childless woman prays with moving lips; the priest thinks she's drunk
727.howItsDone: Jews read Hannah's story as a model of personal prayer, and the Talmud draws from her the way the silent standing prayer, the Amidah, is said: lips moving, voice too low for others to hear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no king, the refrain that closed Judges: every man did what was right in his own eyes. Your line was not just my own eyes. Today a new book opens, with one woman at a sanctuary.

Every year a family travels up to Shiloh to bring an offering, and every year it goes the same way. Elkanah gives portions of the meat to his wife Peninnah and her children, and a double portion to his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves. Hannah has no children. And every year Peninnah provokes her about it, until Hannah weeps and won't eat. Her husband asks, kindly: am I not better to thee than ten sons? It doesn't reach her. So after the meal she goes to the sanctuary and stands before God. An old priest named Eli is sitting by the doorpost, watching.
screen: `EVERY YEAR, UP TO SHILOH.` → `PENINNAH PROVOKES HER.` → `ELI WATCHES FROM THE DOORPOST.`

segments.voice: What Eli sees is strange: a woman, her mouth moving, no sound coming out. "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." Eli decides she's drunk: how long will you be drunken? Put away your wine. The priest at the house of God looks at a woman praying with everything she has, and gets her completely wrong. She doesn't storm off, and she doesn't swallow it. She corrects him. No, my lord. I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but "poured out my soul before the LORD." Don't count me as a worthless woman. Poured out, the way you'd empty a jar. And Eli changes on the spot. He doesn't defend himself. He says, "Go in peace," and adds a blessing: may the God of Israel grant what you asked. Then a line that's easy to miss. Hannah goes her way, eats, and "her countenance was no more sad." Nothing has happened yet, no child, only an old priest's blessing. The text doesn't explain the change; it records it, right after she has said it all to God. The child comes later in the chapter, and she names him Samuel, saying she asked him of the Lord. It starts here, with a woman nobody could hear, and a priest who had to learn to listen.

segments.voice: Think of the thing you carry and rarely say out loud, the one that comes back every year like the trip to Shiloh, and let your lips move with it, your voice too low to hear. If you pray, pour it out to God the way Hannah did; if you don't, just let it be said, all of it, once.

728.title: Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1–10)
728.hook: "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust"
728.howItsDone: Jews read Hannah's song as part of the book of Samuel, among the Prophets; by tradition her story is also read aloud in the synagogue on Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah at Shiloh, lips moving without sound, and a priest who misjudged her. Your line was she spoke in her heart. Today, every word she says.

Hannah brings her son back up to Shiloh. He has been born and weaned, and she leaves him with the same priest to serve, as she promised. Last time, nobody could hear her. This time the text gives us every word. "And Hannah prayed, and said," and what comes out is not a thank-you note. It's a song about the whole world turning over. The mighty fall. The hungry eat. And at its center, one line about where God goes looking for people: "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust."
screen: `THE BOY IS BROUGHT TO SHILOH.` → `THE QUIET WOMAN SINGS.` → `OUT OF THE DUST.`

segments.voice: It starts with her: "My heart exulteth in the LORD." She has been mocked every year by someone with more; now she says her mouth is enlarged over her enemies. Then, almost at once, it stops being about her. The bows of the mighty are broken, and those who stumbled are girded with strength. Those who were full hire themselves out for bread, and the hungry cease to hunger. "The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich; He bringeth low, He also lifteth up." One woman's answered prayer, read as a pattern for everyone. Then the center: "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dung-hill." The lowest places the song can name. And the next words say why: to set them among princes, to make them inherit a seat of honor. Not just rescued. Seated. A psalm says nearly the same words. One more surprise at the end. The song closes with God giving strength to his king and exalting the horn of his anointed. A king. Two days ago, Judges ended with no king in Israel. Hannah sings about a king who doesn't exist yet, and her son, the boy she just handed over, will be the one who anoints him. Some readers hear the whole book of Samuel folded up inside her song.
screen: `MY HEART EXULTETH IN THE LORD.` · `THE MIGHTY FALL, THE HUNGRY EAT.` · `RAISED, AND SEATED AMONG PRINCES.` · `SHE SINGS OF A KING BEFORE THERE IS ONE.` · then, large: `HE RAISETH UP THE POOR OUT OF THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who's low right now, lonely, broke, ignored, left out of the room, and picture where they're sitting. Then ask the song's question: what would it take, not just to help them up, but to give them a seat? If you pray, hold Hannah's line for them: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust.

Hannah's song. The prayer Hannah sings at Shiloh when she gives her son to serve: the mighty fall, the low are raised and seated with princes. It closes a week that ran from the last judges to the first pages of Samuel.
Your line: raised from the dust. Not just a hand up, but a seat. That's the week.
